title: Towards privacy-preserving digital marketing: an integrated framework for user modeling using deep learning on a data monetization platform
summary: Builds a user-modeling pipeline for a consent-based data monetization platform, embedding browsing behaviour into user representations, synthesizing those representations with a customized GAN so that marketing segments can be shared without exposing individuals, and evaluating downstream segmentation and targeting quality. CTGAN is not run: it is described in the related-work survey of tabular GAN variants as the conditional-generator approach to mixed continuous and discrete columns, and named again in future work as a variant the authors suggest trying instead of their own architecture.
evidence: the related-work section surveys GAN variants beyond images and states that another notable variation is CTGAN, which aims to synthesize tabular data consisting of continuous and discrete columns using a conditional generator, adding that CTGAN faces challenges in handling imbalanced discrete columns and complex continuous columns; the synthesis section states that to synthesize user representations while preserving privacy the authors employ a customized GAN architecture of their own rather than an existing tabular model; the limitations and future-work section proposes that future research could investigate variations of GANs such as medWGAN, medBGAN and CTGAN, which places CTGAN as untried prior art; reference 56 is Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni (2019). No CTGAN row appears in any results table

title: Interpretable tabular data generation
summary: Proposes GANBLR, which replaces the neural generator of a tabular GAN with a Bayesian-network classifier so that the generative model exposes explicit feature interactions and per-feature importance, making both the generated data and the generation process interpretable while matching neural models on machine-learning utility. CTGAN is the state-of-the-art benchmark the paper measures itself against, and its mode-specific normalization and training-by-sampling are set out at length as the design GANBLR departs from.
evidence: the introduction names CTGAN, TableGAN and MedGAN as the GAN-based state of the art for tabular generation and states that CTGAN generates tabular data via a conditional GAN-like strategy in which categorical features are treated as a condition; the related-work section states that the current SOTA model for tabular data generation, CTGAN, falls in the auxiliary-classifier stream and that CTGAN leverages mode-specific normalization and training-by-sampling to generate better quality synthetic datasets with both categorical and numeric features, then describes the normalized value being concatenated with categorical features to form CTGAN's input and calls training-by-sampling the key component of CTGAN's generator; section 4.1.2 states the authors compare GANBLR with CTGAN, TableGAN and MedGAN, all trained 150 epochs on the large datasets and 100 on the medium and small ones, and Table 3 reports train-on-synthetic-test-on-real utility for GANBLR against CTGAN across interaction levels. GANBLR's generator is a Bayesian network, so CTGAN's conditional vector is described but not adopted

title: Enhanced classification of hydraulic testing of directional control valves with synthetic data generation
summary: Addresses the cost of end-of-line hydraulic testing for directional control valves, where leakage classes are rare and each labelled sample is expensive, by augmenting a 276-feature test dataset with synthetic records and measuring whether classifier error improves, comparing generative models against SMOTE and against combinations of the two. Three of the four generators evaluated are SDV synthesizers run from the library: CTGAN, CopulaGAN and TVAE, with the paper noting that CopulaGAN is a CTGAN variation provided by SDV and reporting per-model correlation preservation, principal-component coverage and downstream error.
evidence: the background section states that promising developments for tabular data are the conditional tabular GAN (CTGAN) and CopulaGAN, and that CopulaGAN is a variation of CTGAN provided by the SDV library, citing both the CTGAN paper and the SDV paper; the same section credits CTGAN with mode-specific normalization to combat non-Gaussian distributions and describes Xu et al.'s TVAE as the same architecture and preprocessing with a loss function adjusted for tabular data; the results report pairwise Spearman correlations for each generator, noting that TVAE partially preserves them while the two GAN-based methods sit near zero, that only small ranges of the first two principal components are covered by CTGAN and CopulaGAN, and that combining SMOTE with CTGAN significantly decreases the error while it increases the error for TVAE and CopulaGAN; Table 3 reports R2 for each model configuration

title: Efficient mortality prediction for acute respiratory failure: a resource-constrained machine learning approach using MIMIC databases
summary: Builds a mortality predictor for acute respiratory failure that is deliberately cheap to train and deploy, drawing cohorts from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV and testing whether class rebalancing by synthetic generation improves sensitivity, the metric that matters when a false negative is a missed death. All three generators used are SDV synthesizers run from the library: CTGAN, CopulaGAN and TVAE each produce balanced training sets at fixed class ratios, and the reported sensitivity gains across the classifiers rest on their output.
affiliations: National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences

National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences
National University of Computer and Emerging Sciences
evidence: the methods section states that two models were selected for their ability to generate both discrete and continuous values and for transparent implementation, the first being CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019), which generates synthetic data by leveraging conditional information from discrete columns using fully connected networks in generator and discriminator, and CopulaGAN which is built on CTGAN; the same section states that a variational autoencoder called TVAE was developed for tabular generation and that TVAE, available through the SDV library, was used to generate synthetic ARF-related data, and states outright that the sdv library was used for the GANs and VAEs; the results state that CTGAN, CopulaGAN and TVAE produced similar results with TVAE giving the best balance of AUC and F1, that the DNN classifier recorded its best sensitivity under CopulaGAN, and that sensitivity improved by at least 10 per cent for XGBoost and random forest

title: Synthetic Generation of Trip Data: The Case of Smart Card
summary: Tackles the release problem for public-transport smart card records, where tag-on and tag-off pairs are re-identifying and agencies cannot share them, by generating synthetic trip data that preserves the spatial and temporal distributions and the origin-destination structure, then checking that models trained on synthetic data transfer to the real data. CTGAN is the generative model the paper runs, chosen for mixed continuous and discrete columns and non-Gaussian distributions, and set against a Bayesian network; the paper names no library, but its hyperparameter list is the CTGAN package's own constructor arguments.
evidence: the methodology states the authors are particularly interested in Tabular Conditional GAN (CTGAN), an extension of GAN that excels in modelling and generating mixed tabular data of continuous and discrete variables (Xu et al. 2019), and that CTGAN has been shown to outperform other generative methods; the motivating list of data properties cites Xu et al. 2019 for non-Gaussian distributions causing the vanishing gradient problem during normalisation, and for mixed and highly imbalanced multi-modal data; the numerical-experiments section states the authors implement both GAN and BN on South East Queensland Smart Card data with code and generated data deposited openly. The implementation is the sdv-dev CTGAN package rather than a reimplementation: the stated hyperparameters are that package's own constructor arguments verbatim, embedding_dim 128, generator_dim (256,256,256), discriminator_dim (256,256,256), generator_lr and discriminator_lr 2e-4, generator_decay and discriminator_decay 1e-6, and discriminator_steps 1, with epochs and batch_size named in the same form

title: PALSYN: a method for synthetic multi-perspective event log generation with differential private guarantees
summary: Generates synthetic process-mining event logs that carry control-flow, timing and data attributes together under a formal differential-privacy guarantee, using a private autoregressive sequence model with DP-K-Means discretization of numerical attributes and composition theorems to account the privacy budget, and compares trace-level fidelity against PRIPEL. CTGAN is the tabular precedent the discretization is reasoned against rather than a model that is run: the authors state their numerical handling adapts Xu et al.'s method, substituting DP-K-Means for the Gaussian mixture that CTGAN uses.
affiliations: German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence; Universität Trier
German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence; Universität Trier
German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence; Universität Trier
evidence: the introduction places tabular data synthesis (Xu et al. 2019) among the generation tasks the work sits beside; the design rationale states that numerical attributes are discretized during preprocessing and reconstructed during postprocessing, which should provide better statistical preservation of numerical values, citing Xu et al. 2019, and states that this concept shares similarities with techniques used in CTGAN, which leverage Gaussian Mixture Models instead of DP-K-Means; the evaluation states that PALSYN preserves attribute similarity while remaining private by adapting the method proposed by Xu et al. 2019 in its private autoregressive log synthesizer. The compared baseline is PRIPEL and no CTGAN row appears in any results table, so CTGAN's technique is adopted in description only

title: ADHS-EL: Dynamic ensemble learning with adversarial augmentation for accurate and robust network intrusion detection
summary: Proposes an intrusion-detection framework that pairs dynamic undersampling with an improved AdvGAN generating adversarial traffic samples, then trains a dynamically weighted classifier ensemble, arguing that augmenting with adversarial rather than merely minority samples both corrects the decision boundary and hardens the model against evasion. CTGAN is one of the eight imbalance-handling baselines run for comparison, reimplemented from a published architecture rather than taken from a library, and is reported as scoring well on adversarial detection while degrading accuracy through overfitting.
evidence: the related-work section states that prior work used Wasserstein GAN and Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) (Xu et al. 2019) to generate network traffic samples targeting anomalous activities and integrated them into the original dataset; the method section cites Xu et al. 2019 for the claim that fully connected networks can capture all possible correlations between columns of tabular data, which is the authors' stated reason for building their improved AdvGAN generator and discriminator that way; the baselines section lists RUS, ROS, SMOTE, ADASYN, SMOTETomek, CTGAN, WGAN and DUEN, noting that the first five came from imblearn while CTGAN and WGAN were implemented from a published network architecture rather than a package; the results tables carry CTGAN rows on accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and the adversarial metrics, and the discussion states that ADASYN, CTGAN and WGAN score well on AADR but perform poorly on accuracy because adding many malicious samples causes overfitting

title: Multi-omics fusion network for prediction of early recurrence in colorectal liver metastases
summary: Predicts early recurrence after resection of colorectal liver metastases by fusing radiomic, transcriptomic and clinical features in an FT-transformer, working from a single-centre cohort of 129 patients where the sample size is small relative to the dimensionality of RNA sequencing. CTGAN carries that constraint: it synthesizes additional gene-expression instances conditioned on recurrence outcome, generated inside each cross-validation training fold so the test fold stays untouched, and the authors name this augmentation as what makes the cohort tractable.
affiliations: Centre Hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal; Université de Montréal
evidence: the methods state that because RNA sequencing data is intrinsically high-dimensional with a relatively low number of instances, the authors synthesized artificial gene expression instances using CTGAN, described as a variant of the vanilla GAN which generates synthetic tabular data by modeling the probability distribution of its rows and which tackles class imbalance in the discrete columns, here the recurrence status; the same section states the dataset was divided into five folds and that for each fold missing values were imputed and synthetic data generated using CTGAN exclusively within the training fold, leaving the testing fold untouched to prevent contamination; the discussion states that to address the challenge of a limited sample size the authors used CTGAN-based synthetic augmentation to expand the effective sample size and better capture the distribution of transcriptomic data, and that the differential gene expression analysis on the augmented data revealed tumorigenesis-related signals; reference 55 is the CTGAN paper

title: Bee-inspired knowledge transfer: synthesizing data for enhanced deep learning explainability
summary: Attacks the problem of explaining an opaque deep model by transferring its knowledge into a synthetic dataset that a decision tree can then be fitted to, comparing two ways of producing that dataset: a generative route and a Bee-algorithm search route, and measuring how completely each transfers the teacher's behaviour. The generative route, KT-GAN, runs the ctgan package at version 0.7.3 with default parameters as the data generator, so one of the paper's two competing methods is CTGAN used unmodified inside a knowledge-transfer pipeline.
evidence: the background states that for its ability to reliably generate resembled data the conditional tabular-GAN (CT-GAN) algorithm is selected to apply for knowledge-transferred data synthesis in this work, citing reference 26, which is Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni (2019); the method section states that the first of the two proposed techniques, knowledge transfer based on GAN (KT-GAN), applies the model generator from CT-GAN to synthesize tabular data; the parameter settings state that KT-GAN uses the ctgan library in Python version 0.7.3 as data generator with all default parameter settings and epoch set to 100, and the environment section repeats that KT-GAN runs Python 3.9.1 with the ctgan library version 0.7.3. The generator is used as shipped rather than modified, so this is a composite built around CTGAN rather than a variant of it

title: Implementation of ensemble machine learning algorithms on exome datasets for predicting early diagnosis of cancers
summary: Classifies cancer type from whole-exome variant data with an ensemble of standard learners, and confronts a sample size too small for the feature count by augmenting the exome table with synthetic records before training, reporting classifier accuracy before and after. Both generators are Xu et al.'s: CTGAN is run for 300 epochs at batch size 10 with the reported generator and discriminator losses, and TVAE alongside it, with the paper reproducing CTGAN's conditional generator and discriminator equations to explain what it ran.
evidence: the abstract states that a novel method to augment the sample size using a generative adversarial network and a variational autoencoder was employed, reconstructing features and labels to generate the data, and that oversampling raised classifier accuracy; the section headed CTGAN and TVAE implementation on tabular data describes CTGAN as a collection of deep-learning based synthetic data generators for single-table data able to learn from real data and generate synthetic clones with high fidelity, citing reference 64, and then reproduces the conditional generator G(z, cond) and discriminator formulations, stating that the equations represent the network structure of the CTGAN model and that the cond vector represents the condition; the results state that the proposed CTGAN model was trained for 300 epochs with a batch size of 10, after which generator loss was 0.2503 and discriminator loss was -1.4397. Note the paper glosses TVAE as a triplet-based variational autoencoder, which misnames Xu et al.'s tabular VAE
